extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, entomologists, and evolutionary biologists (readers of Nature)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether resemblance among species (especially butterflies and other insects) is due to natural selection and whether it is Batesian, Müllerian, or other forms of mimicry; includes criteria about mechanism, predator perception, geographic co-occurrence, reciprocity, and sex-specific patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic non-identity despite visual similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in outward appearance can be produced by different underlying means (alteration in shape and diminution of scales; diminution in size only; reduction in number of scales; scales becoming transparent and vertically oriented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasizes that identical visual effects produced by different structural changes indicate that the likeness is superficial while the real differences are profound — supporting the view that natural selection can achieve the same visible result by multiple morphological routes. Examples: Ithomiines, Pierines, Danaines, and associated moths produce transparency by different changes to wing scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance must be interpretable in terms of enemy vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The common features of mimetic resemblance 'must stand in relation to vision of some sort' — i.e., resemblance must affect the perceptual apparatus of predators (would-be enemies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion underpins the argument for natural selection acting via predator perception rather than other direct agencies; the author repeatedly frames mimicry as adaptation to predator vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer single adequate cause (Occam's razor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having found an adequate cause (natural selection) for one case of a phenomenon, we should not multiply causes for other similar cases without reason ('Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as methodological principle to argue that Batesian and Müllerian phenomena, when similar in effect, should be examined first under the already-established cause of natural selection before invoking distinct explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive benefit for distasteful forms grouping (need to demonstrate benefit)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must show why it should benefit distasteful forms of various affinities to assemble into homoeochromatic (essentially similar outward aspect) groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as a substantive requirement for the Müllerian hypothesis — the theory needs to explain why mutual resemblance among unpalatable species is advantageous. The historical solution (Müller) and subsequent elaboration by Meldola and Poulton are offered as answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predator learning (Müller’s 'tax' hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Müller's suggestion presumes predators (birds) lack instinctive food discrimination and must learn by experience, so each generation of predators causes a sacrifice (a 'tax') of distasteful individuals before avoidance is learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This learning-based mechanism provides the selective pressure favoring convergent warning signals because resemblance reduces the number of sacrificial trials required per species. Cited historical corroboration (Lloyd Morgan) is used to justify the assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common aposeme reduces predation 'tax' (quantitative benefit of shared warning signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple distasteful species share the same warning colour or aposeme, the number of trials predators must make to learn to avoid them is reduced proportionally, lowering the cost borne by each species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by sugar-plum thought experiments: two distasteful flavours coloured differently require more trials than if both coloured the same; hence shared aposemes confer mutual protection and supply the selective motive for Müllerian association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Batesian vs Müllerian mimicry and allow complementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether resemblance represents Batesian mimicry (palatable mimics copying distasteful models) or Müllerian mimicry (mutually distasteful species sharing warning signals); recognize these theories as supplementary rather than mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author stresses that both types may occur 'beside or within' Müllerian associations and that cases should be classified accordingly rather than forcing exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synaposematism: same warning badge across unrelated taxa in a region
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of a common warning badge ('aposeme') by otherwise unrelated insects in the same geographical area (synaposematism) is significant evidence for selection acting on predator perception rather than on phylogenetic affinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include black-and-yellow wasp bands being emulated by distant taxa (e.g. Cinnabar caterpillars); geographical co-occurrence is important — we do not see the same aposeme shared across distant regions (e.g., Eastern Euploea resembling American Heliconius is not observed). Poulton’s term and arguments are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diaposematism / reciprocity: evidence of mutual influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for reciprocity where two species have each adopted characters of the other (mutual approach by give-and-take), implying both acted as model and mimic (term proposed: 'diaposematism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives examples (Papilio rex and Danaine Melinda formosa; Mylothris and Phrissura) where forewing/hindwing characters appear exchanged, and labels this mutual influence as evidence of Müllerian processes operating reciprocally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in mimicry explained by differential selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When sexes differ in protection, it is usually the female that is better protected; therefore females are more often found in mimetic forms while males remain non-mimetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace's earlier point is cited: female survival (as guardian of brood) is more important to fitness, so females more readily enter mimetic combinations. Examples: Papilio dardanus (non-mimetic male, multiple mimetic female forms), Leuceronia argia, Hypolimnas bolina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Müllerian groups form networks (nexus) rather than isolated clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimetic assemblages in a region are often connected by gradations from group to group, with dominant forms acting as centers but with inter-group links and transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes it is difficult to illustrate in a short lecture but provides routes of stepwise resemblance between Pieris forms and various distasteful groups (e.g., transitions leading to Heliconius patterns) to show the presence of gradations and links among mimicry groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within Müllerian groups subordinate members may influence each other (not only the dominant model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when one species is dominant and widely recognized as a model, subordinate members of the group may show resemblance to each other in ways that suggest they influenced each other — implying some or all may be distasteful and thus the group may be partly or wholly Müllerian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Limnas chrysippus (dominant Danaine) with African Acraea and a lycaenid mimic — the Acraea and lycaenid resemble each other more than either resembles Limnas, suggesting mutual Müllerian influence or multiple distasteful species within the group. Poulton's observations of diverse beetles mimicking mutillid hymenopterans in non-mutilloid traits are cited.
